introduction: “Be thou of the people of hell-fire, but be not a hypocrite.” The saying, quoted by Bahá’u’lláh, sets the tone: open unbelief is preferred to belief that is only on the tongue. The readings describe the type in the Qur’an’s terms, people who say one thing to the believers and another among themselves, illustrate it with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s stories of courtiers and of drunkards protesting against drink, and advise keeping a distance. The Gospels’ sayings against the Pharisees and the Apocalypse’s “neither cold nor hot” are the same judgment. The parable of the tares, and the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like other men, turn the question back on whoever is doing the judging.
questions: Why would hypocrisy be worse than unbelief?
How can one recognize hypocrisy in oneself?
The readings advise avoiding hypocrites; the parable advises not pulling up the tares. How would you apply both?

outside.why: “Be thou an unbeliever, but be not a hypocrite.” I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Courtiers bowing: “Most wonderful, Sire!” The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart.
Like drunkards gathered together to protest against the drinking of alcohol. They say, and do not.
Good intention does not accept dissimulation. Hamlet: one may smile, and smile, and be a villain.
Outwardly one word, inwardly another. This people honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.
Professing with words, denying with deeds. Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Calling on the All-Merciful with the tongue. Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom.
Claiming with the tongue what is not in the heart. Let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.
Attributing themselves to the All-Merciful, acting otherwise. Whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward.

Love to all, but close companionship only with the sincere. In the parable the servants who want to pull up the tares are told: nay; lest ye root up also the wheat. Who is able to tell a hypocrite from a struggler, and what follows if no one is?
The reading quotes the Qur’an on those who say “we believe” to believers and otherwise to others; the same book advises: sit not with them until they engage in some other conversation.
Even teaching can be done for show. That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret.
Professing love with craft. Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
Avoid the hypocrite. The Pharisee in the parable thanked God he was not as other men are. How does a person who shuns hypocrites avoid becoming him?
